title: Which case interview framework should I use? A simple way to choose
description: How to pick the right framework for any case: the three families of case questions, the eleven core frameworks and which case types they fit.
hook: One of the most common worries is "which framework do I use?" The honest answer is that you do not need to memorise dozens. Most case questions fall into three families, and once you know which family you are in, the structure follows. Here is how to tell.
body:
Every case question is really one of three kinds. Work out which kind you have, and you already know the shape of a good answer.

Diagnose: "Why is this happening, and how do we fix it?"

Break the problem into parts that add up, find which part moved, then fix that part.

  • How can the client make more profit? Profits are falling, or the client wants them higher.
  • How can the client cut costs? The client needs to cut costs, often by a target percentage.
  • How can the client improve this process? Operations cases: something is slow, costly or error-prone.

Decide: "Should we do this?"

Test it against a few yes/no questions, put a number on it, and end with a clear yes or no.

  • How should the client respond to a rival's move? A rival cuts prices, launches a product or enters the market.
  • Should the client enter this market? A new country, customer segment or product category.
  • Should the client make this investment? A new plant, more capacity, a system, a store or a piece of equipment.
  • Should the client buy this company? A company buying another company (mergers and acquisitions).
  • Should the fund invest in this company? Private equity: a fund buys a company to improve it and sell it in 3 to 7 years.

Generate: "How can we do this?"

Lay out every option in buckets that don't overlap, size them, then pick the best few.

  • How can the client grow? The client wants more revenue and is open to options.
  • How should the client launch the product? The client wants a plan to launch a product. If the question is whether to launch at all, use market entry.
  • What price should the client charge? Setting or changing a price.

Smaller tools to keep in your pocket

  • Market sizing: "How big is the market for X?" Say your approach before any maths.
  • Where costs hide (value chain): Use with "How to reduce costs?" to find specific levers in each part of the business.
  • The 3Cs: A quick strategic scan when you need a starting structure for an open question.
  • Five forces (Porter): How attractive is this industry? Useful inside market entry and acquisitions.
  • The 4Ps (marketing mix): The "What to offer" branch of a product launch.
  • Pricing methods: Ways to set a price once you know the floor and the ceiling.
  • Build, partner or buy?: How to get into a new market or capability.
  • Outsource or keep in-house?: Make-or-buy questions in operations and cost cases.
  • Risk checklist: When you are asked "What are the risks?" or need to close a recommendation.
  • "How would you find that out?": When the interviewer asks how you would get data.
  • Simple splits for brainstorming: When you need buckets fast for "What else could they do?"

By case type

  • Profitability. Ask first: Is the whole industry hit, or just us?
  • Revenue drop. Ask first: Which stream, segment or region is falling?
  • Market entry. Ask first: What is the goal, and over what time frame?
  • Growth strategy. Ask first: Growth from where: revenue split by business unit?
  • M&A. Ask first: Why does the client want to buy?
  • Private equity. Ask first: What return does the fund need, and over how long?
  • Pricing. Ask first: What is the product worth to the customer?
  • Competitive response. Ask first: How big is the threat in revenue terms?
  • Investment / capacity. Ask first: Is demand real, and can existing capacity be squeezed?
  • Cost & operations. Ask first: Goal: lower cost, more capacity, or reliability?
  • Market sizing. Ask first: Units or value? Which geography? Any limiting factor?
  • Product launch. Ask first: Is the decision to launch made, and what must the launch achieve?
  • Valuation. Ask first: Valuing a standalone business or a stream of cash flows?
  • Public sector. Ask first: What does success look like for citizens and for the budget?
  • Product: design. Ask first: Who is it for, and what does success mean?
  • Product: improve / grow. Ask first: Improve on which measure (engagement, revenue, UX)?
  • Product: metric drop. Ask first: How is it measured, since when, sudden or gradual?

A word on memorising

Interviewers have heard the standard frameworks hundreds of times. What impresses them is a structure that clearly fits this client. Learn the families and the core trees, then practise adapting them. The structuring guide shows how.
outro: You do not have to get all of this right at once. Pick one thing from this guide to focus on in your next practice case.
